problem: Target-driven visual navigation with plain deep RL (e.g. TD-A3C) is sample-inefficient and generalizes poorly to unseen scenes and novel targets, because goal information is hard-coded and the agent never models how actions change its observations.
motivation: A navigating agent must infer which parts of the current view matter for the target, and must understand the causal link between its actions and the resulting change in observation. The paper injects this understanding through an information-theoretic regularizer instead of relying on reward alone.
key_idea: Add to the A3C objective a mutual-information regularizer between action and next observation given the current observation. It is implemented as a conditional VAE that imagines the next observation from the current view and the target, and the action is predicted from the current and imagined observations.
insight: Imagining the next observation and acting on the difference beats direct image-to-action mapping: the ablation without generation (Ours-NoGen) is worse (41.2 vs 45.7 SR), and a stochastic latent beats a deterministic one. Over-regularizing the latent with a standard normal prior hurts (VallinaGen 37.5 SR), so a learned conditional prior is needed. Using the value loss only as an auxiliary task on shared layers matters (NoVal 34.9 SR). It also helps with stop-action data imbalance, and multi-view input makes generation easier than front-view (FroView 32.3).
method: Task/reward setup: 4-view RGB observation (300x300), image goal, discrete grid-graph actions (move fwd/back/left/right, rotate cw/ccw, stop). Reward is +10 on success, -0.01 per step, -0.2 on collision, plus geodesic-distance shaping.

MI regularizer: a lower bound on I(a_t; x_{t+1}|x_t) decomposed into three terms: predictive control (action log-likelihood given x_t and x_{t+1}), reconstruction of the ground-truth next observation, and KL. Shortest-path (A*) ground-truth next observation and action provide supervision.

Conditional VAE generator: posterior q(z|x_t,g) is trained to match a prior p(z|x_t,a_t^gt) computed from the ground-truth action. z decodes to a next-state feature s_{t+1} (a 512-D CNN feature, not pixels).

Policy head: predicts a_t from the current state feature f(x_t), the imagined s_{t+1} and the previous action a_{t-1} (which reduces back-and-forth motion). The loss is L_p = α·(-log p(a)) + β·||s_{t+1} - f(x^gt_{t+1})||² + γ·KL, with α=1, β=0.01, γ=1e-4.
Value as auxiliary task: the value loss (weight ω=0.5) only updates the shared layers, rather than serving as the TD baseline for the policy gradient. It helps with stop-action imbalance.
Training: A3C with 6 workers, RMSprop with lr 1e-4, spectral-norm CNN, curriculum over scene categories on AI2-THOR (60h on AVD, 120h on AI2-THOR, 1080Ti).

setting.backbone: Custom CNN + VAE + MLP actor-critic (trained from scratch, A3C)
setting.training_data: AI2-THOR: 80 training scenes with about 18k target views; AVD: 8 training scenes with 120 selected target views; supervised by shortest-path ground-truth actions and next observations plus RL reward; no extra data
setting.observation: four-view RGB (0/90/180/270°) 300x300 plus target image; also RGB/depth/semantic variants
setting.action_space: discrete grid-graph: move fwd/back/left/right, rotate cw/ccw, stop (converted to wheel velocities on TurtleBot)
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR; Active Vision Dataset (real captured discrete scenes); real TurtleBot
setting.privileged: none at test time (shortest-path supervision and GT next observations used only in training)

results: On unseen AI2-THOR scenes the method reaches 45.7 SR / 25.8 SPL with known targets and 37.7 / 20.5 with novel targets, at least 10% higher SR than NeoNav and GSP (34.4 / 27.5 SR). On AVD it gets 23.1 SR vs GSP 19.3, and on the real TurtleBot 28% vs GSP 24%. With a class-label goal on AI2-THOR it beats SAVN (45.8 vs 41.9 SR).
limitations: Needs expert shortest-path supervision from topology graphs of training scenes
Real-world collision rate stays high (40%) and success is low (28%) in continuous space with a discrete-trained policy; results on AVD show higher variance
Evaluated only in static environments with discrete grid-graph actions and only small training sets (8 AVD scenes)
